It's good but it needs one very important change. The special ability button should not be Q. It means you can't move left while using it. This becomes important in some lategame builds where you can have 100% special ability spam uptime. Greatly stops your ability to actually move! Needs to be a key that isn't used by a WASD finger, or even better, rebindable (even if rebinding keys is against the spirit of a PS1 game). edit: nvm see comments, you can use it with RMB as well. PS: game is VERY light on content. Fine for the price but after a few hours you'll have tried everything the game has to offer. Also kind of an illusion of build variety, it really boils down to: build to trigger crits to roid your weapons OR build to trigger crits to spam your damage type-matched ability OR build to trigger crits to spam Aegis and boosts. Not hating, this is an impressive one person little project, but the content of the other reviews is universally positive and this should be mentioned. I have endgame achievements that 1% of players have in less than 4 hours of game time.. I have explored all that the game has to offer pretty quickly. There is also significant imbalance between the characters. A fun Saturday afternoon for 7 bucks, but probably won't play it again unless it gets additional content.

There comes a point where you gotta ask yourself "is a game good just because it's a really efficient dopamine factory?" Vital Shell presents an answer to the genre of these vampire survivor-likes. There are so many things about it that feel more "good for the brain". level-ups are rewarded after waves of enemies are completed, progression is paced out better with fewer rapidly-given upgrades, gameplay is more engaging and skill-focused so the rewards you do get feel more earned and satisfying... I could go on. Being a rogue-lite, Vital Shell is still inherently engaging and addicting, but it feels less so like a parasite that I need to feed every day, and more like a fulfilling and genuinely fun experience I want to come back to. Not to mention the vibes are immaculate. It may vary person-to-person how "aesthetic"y the game feels, but there are times where I really believe this could've been a game made by an artsy Japanese dude who loves twin-stick shmups in the 90s. The jungle OST is also a pretty unique direction for the genre, and I love me some good drum n bass. As a character designer, I also think the less-is-more approach to the visual character designs is highly effective, with strong shapes and silhouettes for both the enemies and the playable mechs. Overall... thank god this game came out when it did because I needed a less parasitic alternative to Megabonk. Highly reccommend, awesome game, will definitely be playing regularly. EDIT: wanna make clear that I'm saying the game is less addictive in a potentially harmful way than other games of the genre. Vital Shell is definitely still addictive, I say as I now pursue the 100% achievement. EDIT AGAIN: So I have since completed 100% of the game's achievements. I was so sad to say goodbye to vital shell, but then I realized... The game lets me have two save files. I could 100% the game AGAIN.

You are twelve. As rain clouds are getting closer, you and your mate are walking aimlessly in the neighborhood, contemplating whether you want to play games on your fake Nintendo called a Polystation that your parents purchased at the flea market. You were thinking, maybe this time when the cartridge that says 100 in 1 games is put in, it might actually have more games that don’t suck, not just 5 bad ones with different names. But suddenly you had a better idea. What if you try to get into your other friend's house, the one you didn't like that much because he never let you play, but at least you can still watch him? You hoped that maybe this time it would be different and he would finally let you play his PS1. You knock on your other mate's door and their mother lets you in, but she says you ought to stay only an hour because your mate didn't do his homework. When you get in, he is playing a strange game. Robots are dancing around in a small square shooting other smaller robots, and there is a huge counter in the middle. As it goes down, more and more enemies get on the screen. The techno music is pumping you up. Everything is blowing up, the robot's weapon is upgraded, boom, everything is dead on the screen. Suddenly your mate sees you and he is not happy. He just wants to play his new game that his parents rented from the local store and you just messed up his plans. You wanted to play just one run, just 30 seconds to feel the rush that can be seen in your mate's eyes, but he says, "Oh, the PS is too hot, we have to wait so it cools down, we cannot play today." Then you suddenly realize why you hate his guts. Of course you never played the game back then. The shop they rented from was waiting for them to return it and you never got a turn. This game feels like traveling back to that time, but instead of the guy saying you cannot play, you could and had the time of your life. Totally worth it, easy 10/10.

If this were a AAA we’d have to be paying $40 for that feature. Free content is always good! Only thing I wanted to point out was the soundtrack in the worlds, don’t get me wrong I liked it, but I wish there was more variety of the dark jungle type music in each map—that can easily be resolved with some future updates (only reason I have it a 9.5/10 for soundtrack). I wanted to gatekeep this game from the normies, but our boy MarvinWizard needs that bread to improve this game and create more awesome and unique games like this in the future. Can’t wait for future updates! And still this game is Just a game ass game 😎 Where I’m still gonna be spending ALL of my off days playing this game for ungodly amounts of hours straight while playing early 2000’s dark jungle tracks, the early days of Linkin Park, and other YouTube videos in the back. Gameplay: 10/10 Music and Soundtrack: 9.5/10 Replay Value: 10/10 Graphics: Nostalgic How it runs: Smooth as butter Hardware required: N64 and PS1 Chance of getting addicted: Intervention might be needed Onto 100%!!!

I play quite a few bullet heaven games, so when I saw this one I was interested, particularly for the music. My main gripe of the game is I find it really hard to look at, it feels like it is running at 20fps or less, despite the framerate counter telling me it is 120fps. I tried it on two different PC's, one a very min spec for gaming and another pretty high spec and it is exactly the same on both. I wondered if my brain or my monitor was playing tricks on me, so I loaded up Yet Another Zombie Survivors and even though it has a 1000x the graphical fidelity of this, it is smooth as butter for my eyes. The game doesn't have the depth or longevity of most bullet heaven games, and certainly nowhere near the top examples. Music wise, I am a big Jungle and Drum&Bass fan since '92, there are some good tracks in here, but I would rate the quality spread of tracks from about 3 to 7 out of 10, there are a lot of lame shovelware D&B tracks included. It isn't a bad game, but it feels more like an alpha prototype for something good, but isn't fleshed out enough for me to recommend it.

MEH...pass... I was expecting arcade fun, which this does supply somewhat, but it just got boring far too quickly. Almost decided to request a refund but I was in the middle of a run...oh well it's not like it was pricey. ===== THE GOOD ====== + Easy to pick up and play because it's arcadey + Kind of fun...for a while ===== THE MEH ====== - Okay so at first I kinda liked the dnb jams, but after playing longer it's pretty annoying and repetitive. There's one song in particular that goes on and on, lasting the course of like...5 enemy waves. Doot-doo doot-doo *drumloop* Doot-doo doot-doo *drumloop*. Deet-da-doo-doo *drumloop*. - It's a little too mindless. Just move around and shoot. By default there's auto-shoot/auto-targetting so all you do is move around in the small square arena. - The graphics are a little too barebones, especially the weapon models. - Nothing really has any OOMF to it, making all weapons/abilities kinda unsatisfying to use. - Replayability seems really low. Not much to work towards. I'll tackle a few more achievements and then shelf this one for good. Meh.

Vital Shell shows a character moving through areas while enemies appear and approach on the screen. The player presses buttons to attack and avoid damage. Enemies disappear when they receive enough hits. The character has a visible health value that decreases when damage is taken. Attacks create effects that can be seen. Movement happens across the environment in different directions. Sometimes the character pauses briefly as if considering existence before continuing to fight as everything remains visible on screen.

Honestly? No, at least not in it's current state. The music and style is novel and a breath of fresh air, but it gets old quite fast. There is not too much content available and it generally wasn't very challenging or felt that fun. I ended up beating all levels in a row and unlocking all the characters in a single session. Look at all the other reviewers playtime despite their praise, see the playtime is not even close to the likes of other survivor-likes out there. This is a game you may play for an evening or a couple days and drop it, if you feel like that's worth it - it's up to you.

As an arcade gamer, it would make sense socially for me to not give this game a recommendation due to it being yet another vampire survivors adjacent game that trends towards being more of a dopamine-hamster-wheel experience than a legit, real game. Vital Shell DOES do enough to differentiate itself, but I won’t pretend it’s a great game. However, For $5, you could do worse, even as an arcade gamer. For one, it does have an arcade mode, and it’s not bad. No pick 3 system in that mode- Just build out your mech’s stats and loadout before the run, and then survive as long as possible. This mode is surprisingly effective. It’s not balanced, of course. Some builds will be astronomically better, and there will be an optimal best build. This mode loops like a loopable arcade game with a roughly 6-8 minute loop cycle, and the game gets fairly challenging pretty quickly, which is what a good arcade game should do. Clearing 2 loops is among the top end of survivability, but I’m sure experts could push further; with some builds, 1 loop would be an achievement. The gameplay loop is typical twin stick gameplay, but it’s snappy, there’s a lot to dodge, and it’s actually fairly satisfying fundamentally with the variety in enemy hitboxes, sheer density, and speed of the combat. The only real downside to it is, like usual, the over-reliance on enemies that track you and subsequent optimal play revolving heavily around circle strafing. More could’ve been done to break this up and create more dynamic movement through the stage, but as the difficulty ramps up, it begins to become more strategic in how you kite enemies, save resources, collect the sparks and so on. Eventually it does get so difficult that the chance of instantly dying begins to spike. This isn’t inherently bad, but it could’ve been slightly tuned away from that without having to lower your damage output and build more towards increased max health. I won’t really comment on the rest of the game much; the campaign is a more typical vampire survivors affair. Banal, padded gameplay more centered around picking the right stats than actual gameplay. Too easy and exploitable difficulty in the campaign. There is also another arcade weekly challenge mode with randomized criteria, and is a good reason to keep playing, if not just sticking with the standard endless arcade mode. As for the stat/build/weapon systems. It’s not doing anything cool or interesting— life stealing is a strong part of the meta and is OP as expected to allow you to face tank a lot of hits and simply survive much easier. I wouldn’t buy it if you’re into interesting build crafting. The combat manages to feel good enough which is what actually matters. For a few bucks, Vital Shell won’t blow anyone’s hair back. Its strong PA1 aesthetics, punchy game feel, and solid enough arcade mode offerings elevate it above your typical vampire survivors/hall of torments into something genuine/core gamers can chew on, at least for a bit before getting bored. The game would be considerably stronger if developed more as a true arcade game, but yeah, if you have a few bucks to spend it’s not a bad title to add to your library

I'm certainly sold on this game. And you'll probably like it too, if you're a fan of this type of action roguelite. It reminds me a lot of Brotato or Vampire Survivors, but with mech suits. And I can't think of many ways to improve those games more than making the player a mech suit pilot. I'm also a big fan of the early 3D era aesthetic. The menus look like something you'd see on a PS1 Demo Disc, and the graphics seem to occupy a space somewhere between PS1 and PS2 era. Even the boss intro scenes have that early 3D pre-rendered look. It's not perfect, though. With games like this you have to be careful that you put enough information into the menus between rounds. And I feel like Vital Shell could use a few more menu tooltips. In particular, some reminder text for the Resonance system. The way that Resonance works, is that each weapon has 4 upgrade slots that are filled with gems of different colors, that provide various bonuses. And when all of the slots are filled, the weapon gets some new property, depending on which combination of gems are slotted in. Thankfully, there's not a Resonance for every possible combination, but it feels like there's enough that some reminder text when you're picking upgrades would be helpful. I played this game for a good chunk of time, and I probably couldn't tell you off the top of my head what the majority of which combinations give which properties. Other than that, I have few complaints. A few weapons have some scalings that you might not intuit from the start, but that's kind of the fun of a game like this - experimenting around and finding your favorite combinations and synergies. Overall, it's a great value for $6. Definitely recommend giving it a try.

In recent years, the low-poly aesthetic reminiscent of the PlayStation 1 era has been growing in popularity—whether in music videos, 3D models shared on social media, or even actual video games. It’s particularly striking that more and more people are discovering From Software’s PS1 lineup—whether it’s King’s Field or Armored Core—and this inspiration has given rise to heartfelt projects like Lunacid and Vital Shell. “But we have Armored Core at home!” Our subject today certainly can’t deny that the development team is crazy about Armored Core. And really, as soon as you launch the game, it’s hard not to confuse it with the AC1 title screen. And within that, the menu has been replicated exactly—it really feels like you’re browsing through the Raven’s Nest database—complete with a memory card, just like on the PS1. How can I describe Vital Shell? Take Armored Core and Gauntlet Legends, mix in a little fantasy, and turn it into an arcade-style experience. The very first trailer had me sold, and although I was a little wary because of the Vampire Survivors comparison, I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. And to my greatest surprise, the very chill, almost atmospheric jungle fits this chaotic, at times suffocating game incredibly well. What I really liked was that the game has a color-based playstyle and character identity, so after a while, based on that, you’ll know which gem boosts which stat, how an opponent moves and tries to make life difficult for us, or what kind of equipment the mech we’ve chosen is equipped with. You’ll need to skillfully maneuver your mech to dodge and eliminate enemies that get weirder and weirder, while the game automatically fires your weapons—and if you don’t trust the AI, you have the option to aim manually. It’s simple—honestly, nothing earth-shattering—but you can play with one hand while eating a Pizza Hut pizza with the other. Reminds me of Earthbound... Currently, there are five different classes available, all of which embody classic fantasy archetypes (e.g., knight, mage, archer), and there are five levels where 20 waves of enemies and an end-of-level boss await us. After defeating enemies, you can collect experience crystals, and after each wave—provided you’ve leveled up—you’ll have the chance to choose what to boost: health, armor, speed, block chance, range, etc. Vital Shell encourages you to experiment and try a new build with every run. Don’t get discouraged for a moment if you get a “game over,” because after every successful or even unsuccessful attempt, your Devotion meter will increase: There are 5 categories here, each with 10 levels, where you can unlock and integrate permanent upgrades, new weapons, gems, and level-up bonuses into the main game. I’m trying to be fair to the game because, for one thing, it just debuted (keep in mind, I mainly played this back in January), and for another, it’s in Early Access. In terms of its concept, Vital Shell is a home run for me, but the truth is that there isn’t enough content yet to keep you hooked for more than a few hours before you get up and look for something else to do. I’m optimistic, though, because the feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, which hopefully bodes well for a bright, content-rich future for the game.

If you get this game and enjoy it, refund it before it's too late and go get Brotato instead. This is that game but with far less content, a camera angle that makes projectiles harder to dodge, and a MUCH more rigid (and frankly boring) weapon selection/stat/upgrade system. The biggest omission is the shop/item-buying phase. If you're familiar with Brotato, imagine "Brotato without the shop/items". Your most frequent picks are comparable to Brotato's 'level up' stat boosts but without more powerful rarities. I.E if one of your upgrade options is Attack Speed it's going to be 5% every time. More interesting effects like 'leave a fire patch if you kill an enemy with a crit' come at fixed intervals and you only get 3-4 per run. The last upgrade mechanic is gems, which seem like a neat idea: grant a 1-3 levels worth of stats to a single weapon, then when you add the fourth and final gem, grant that weapon a bonus effect based on the color combination. Not all color combos have effects: 4 Red grants you the 'Detonation' effect, but since 'Red Red Blue Green' doesn't have an effect, the game just takes those 2 Red gems and gives Detonation again. Unfortunately, most of the combo effects are bad, boring, or both, and often deal a damage type your mech/build is a poor match for. Meta progression comes from the game's "Devotions". You gain 'EXP' to level them up at the end of each run, and each level grants a small boost for all future runs. By 'small' I mean on the scale of "2% attack speed". I don't really know how deep these get because I've only gotten one to level 5 and I'm already bored out of my mind and won't be playing it again. Needs a LOT more time in the oven.
